blocks.md:
- Describe what a beat (pulse) is and feel it by tapping or playing at the piano.
- Explain what a bar is and why beats are grouped into bars.
- Identify bar lines, including the final bar line, on a piece of written music.
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md: Recap: the **beat** is the steady, even pulse that runs through music, like a ticking clock or a heartbeat. It is what you tap your foot to. It can be fast or slow, but it stays even. In this lesson we look at how beats carry different **weight** (strong and weak), how they group into **bars**, and the **bar lines** that mark those groups on the page.

Not all beats feel the same. Even when beats are perfectly even in time, some feel heavier or more important than others. Musicians call these **strong beats** and **weak beats**.

A strong beat has a natural weight or emphasis to it. A weak beat feels lighter, like it is leaning towards the next strong beat. This push and pull between strong and weak beats is what gives music its sense of movement and groove.

**Strong beat:** a beat that feels heavy or accented.

**Weak beat:** a beat that feels lighter, less accented.

A very common pattern in music uses four beats in a row, counted **1, 2, 3, 4**. In this pattern:

- Beat **1** is the strongest beat.
- Beat **2** is weak.
- Beat **3** has a little weight, but less than beat 1.
- Beat **4** is weak, and it leads you back to beat 1 again.

So the pattern feels like: **ONE**, two, three, four, **ONE**, two, three, four.

Say this aloud and clap along, making beat 1 just a tiny bit louder than the others:

**ONE** - two - three - four - **ONE** - two - three - four

Notice how your voice naturally wants to land more firmly on **ONE**. That is the strong beat.
blocks.title: Feeling the strong beat in a four-beat count

blocks.md: Now take this to the keyboard. You are going to play one note, middle C, once on each beat.

blocks.label: Middle C (C4) is the note you will play

blocks.md:
**Step 1.** Place your right-hand thumb on middle C.

**Step 2.** Count aloud: "1, 2, 3, 4" at a slow, steady pace, like a clock.

**Step 3.** Press middle C once on each beat. On beat **1**, press a little firmer so the note sounds slightly louder. On beats 2, 3, and 4, press more gently.

**Step 4.** Keep going for several rounds: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4.

As you play, listen. Does beat 1 feel like a natural "landing" point? Does beat 4 feel like it is pulling you forward to the next 1? That feeling is the strong and weak beats.

blocks.label: Four beats on middle C: beat 1 strong (louder), beats 2, 3, 4 weak

blocks.md: You do not have to press hard on beat 1. Even a small difference in finger pressure makes the strong beat clear. Gentle control matters more than force.
The four-beat pattern you just used (1, 2, 3, 4) is one of the most common in all of music. You will meet it again very soon when we look at how beats are grouped into bars.

C C C C
blocks.caption: Four beats in a row on middle C. All four notes are the same length, but they do not all feel the same. Beat 1 is the strong beat.

items.prompt: In a four-beat count (1, 2, 3, 4), which beat is the strongest?
items.explain: Beat 1 is the strongest beat in a four-beat pattern. It is where the music naturally lands with the most weight.
options: Beat 2
Beat 3
Beat 4
Beat 1

items.prompt: In music, all beats feel exactly the same because they are evenly spaced in time.
items.explain: Even though beats are evenly spaced, they do not all feel the same. Some beats are strong (heavier, more accented) and others are weak (lighter). This difference is what gives music its sense of movement.

items.prompt: After tapping middle C on beats 1, 2, 3, and 4, did beat 1 feel different to you? How would you describe the feeling in your own words?

blocks.title: Check your understanding: Strong and Weak Beats

blocks.md:
Beats do not just go on forever in a long, undivided stream. We gather them into small, equal packages. Each package is called a **bar** (some books use the word **measure**, which means exactly the same thing and is most typically used in American English).

Every bar holds the same number of beats as the one before it. That sameness is what gives music its steady, predictable feel.
**Bar (or measure):** a small, equal group of beats that repeats throughout a piece of music.
Think of bars like fence posts along a road. The posts are evenly spaced, and the gap between each pair of posts is exactly the same size. Each gap is one bar.

Most of the music you will meet early on groups beats in one of two ways:

- **Four beats per bar.** This is sometimes called "common time" and it is everywhere, from pop songs to hymns.
- **Three beats per bar.** This is the feel of a waltz. It has a flowing, rolling quality.

Both groupings are shown below on the stave. Notice the "4" and "3" written at the start of each line. That number tells you how many beats fit in each bar. (You will learn much more about this symbol, called the **time signature**, in a later lesson. For now, just notice that it sits right at the beginning and tells us the grouping.)

blocks.md: Let's listen to four beats played one after another, using the notes C, D, E, and F. These four notes sit next to each other on the white keys, starting at middle C.

blocks.label: C, D, E, F: the four notes you will play
One bar of four beats: C, D, E, F

blocks.md: Now hear two bars in a row. Notice how arriving back on C at the start of each group feels like a small moment of arrival, like taking a breath.

blocks.label: Two bars of four beats: C D E F, C D E F

blocks.md:
As you listen (or play), try counting quietly out loud: **1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4**.

The number 1 always lands on C. That first beat of the bar tends to feel slightly stronger than the others. You will explore exactly why in the next section.
blocks.title: Feeling the grouping

blocks.text: Now Try It at the Piano

blocks.md:
**Step 1.** Find middle C with your right hand. Place your thumb (finger 1) on C, index finger (finger 2) on D, middle finger (finger 3) on E, and ring finger (finger 4) on F.

**Step 2.** Play C, D, E, F one note at a time, slowly and evenly. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" as you go.

**Step 3.** When you reach F, go straight back to C and repeat the group. Do this four or five times without stopping.

**Step 4.** Try to make every beat exactly the same length. Steady and even is the goal, not fast.

Can you feel the moment when you arrive back on C? That arrival point is the beginning of a new bar.
If keeping a steady pace feels tricky, try nodding your head once for each note as you play. Your body's natural sense of rhythm will help your hands stay even.

blocks.text: Now Hear Three Beats Per Bar

blocks.md: Now compare that four-beat feel with a three-beat grouping. Listen to C, D, E repeated as bars of three. Notice how the pattern feels slightly different. It lifts and rolls rather than marching steadily forward.

blocks.label: Two bars of three beats: C D E, C D E

blocks.md: You do not need to memorise both groupings right now. The important idea is simply this: beats are always gathered into equal groups, and those groups are called bars. The number of beats per bar can change from piece to piece, but within any one piece it usually stays the same all the way through.

items.prompt: What is a bar (also called a measure)?
items.explain: A bar is a small, equal package of beats. Every bar in a piece holds the same number of beats as the one before it.
options: A single beat on its own
A small, equal group of beats that repeats throughout a piece
The speed at which beats are played
A symbol written at the start of a line of music

items.prompt: In a piece of music, different bars can hold different numbers of beats.
items.explain: Within a single piece, every bar holds the same number of beats. The grouping stays consistent all the way through.

items.prompt: When you play C, D, E, F as four even beats and then repeat the group, what does each group of four represent?
items.explain: Each group of four even beats is one bar. The bar is the container that holds those four beats together as one complete unit.
options: A time signature
A scale
One bar
One beat

blocks.text: Bar Lines and What They Do

blocks.md:
You have learned that beats are grouped into bars. But how does a musician know, just by looking at the page, where one bar ends and the next begins?

The answer is the **bar line**.

A bar line is a vertical line, a straight line drawn from top to bottom, that cuts across the stave. The **stave** is the set of five horizontal lines that music is written on. Every time a bar is full, a bar line is drawn to close it off and signal the start of the next bar.
**Bar line:** a vertical line drawn across the stave that marks the end of one bar and the start of the next.
Think of bar lines like the lines between the verses of a poem. They do not change the music itself. They simply divide it into tidy, equal groups so it is easy to follow.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F | G A B c | e d c B | G4
blocks.caption: A simple four-bar melody in 4/4 time. Each bar holds four beats. The vertical lines crossing the stave are bar lines.

blocks.md: Look at the notation above. You can see the five lines of the stave running across the page. You can also see three vertical lines cutting through those five lines. Each of those vertical lines is a bar line.

blocks.label: Listen to the four-bar melody above, one note at a time

blocks.md: As you listen, try tapping your finger on the desk: one tap per note. Feel how the notes fall into groups of four. Each group of four is one bar. The bar line on the page marks the moment you begin a fresh group.

Sit at your piano and play these four notes slowly, one after another: **C, D, E, F**. Count out loud: one, two, three, four. That is one bar. Now play **G, A, B, C** and count again: one, two, three, four. That is a second bar. Notice that nothing sounds different at the bar line. The bar line is simply a visual marker on the page. It helps you keep your place in the music.

blocks.label: The notes used in bar 1 (C D E F) and bar 2 (G A B C)

items.prompt: What is a bar line?
items.explain: A bar line is a vertical line crossing the stave. It closes off one bar and signals the start of the next. The horizontal lines are the stave itself, not bar lines.
options: A horizontal line that music notes sit on
A vertical line drawn across the stave that marks the end of one bar and the start of the next
A symbol that tells you how fast to play
A rest that lasts for a whole bar

items.prompt: A piece of music has 5 bar lines drawn across the middle of the stave. How many bars does it contain?
items.explain: There is always one more bar than the number of bar lines in the middle. Five bar lines create six bars: one before the first line, four between the lines, and one after the last line.
options: 4 bars
5 bars
6 bars
7 bars

items.prompt: A bar line changes the sound of the music at the point where it appears.
items.explain: A bar line is only a visual marker on the page. It helps you read and keep your place in the music, but it makes no difference to how the music sounds.

blocks.md:
You have already learned the ordinary bar line. It is a single thin vertical line that separates one bar from the next. It means: **one bar has ended, the next one begins**. The music keeps going.

Now we have its close relative: the **final bar line**.
**Final bar line:** two vertical lines placed side by side at the very end of a piece. The first line is thin and the second line is thick. Together they mean: **the music is finished**.
Think of it like the last full stop at the end of a book. The final bar line is the definitive full stop that tells you to stop playing.

Here is a one-bar phrase followed by an ordinary bar line, then a second bar, then a final bar line at the end.

- The thin single line in the middle separates the two bars. Music continues past it.
- The thin-plus-thick pair at the very end is the final bar line. Music stops there.
blocks.title: Ordinary bar line vs. final bar line

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F | G A B c |]
blocks.caption: Two bars of notes. The single vertical line in the middle is an ordinary bar line. The thin-and-thick pair at the right end is the final bar line. The piece ends there.

blocks.md: Do not confuse the final bar line with an ordinary bar line that happens to be at the end of a line on the page. If the second stroke is NOT thicker than the first, the music continues on the next line. Only the thin-then-thick pair means the piece is truly over.
Here is a slightly longer example. Read through it and find the final bar line at the end.

blocks.label: Listen to the three-bar phrase above, played as a sequence

blocks.md:
Sit at your piano and play those three bars yourself, using the notation above as your guide.

1. Start on E above middle C.
2. Play through all three bars at a slow, steady pace.
3. When you reach the final bar line, stop. Do not play any further notes.

blocks.label: The notes used in the example: E, F, G, A, B (starting from E above middle C)

items.prompt: What does the final bar line look like?
items.explain: The final bar line is always a thin line first, then a thicker line right beside it. This specific combination signals the end of the piece.
options: Two thin vertical lines of equal thickness
One thin vertical line on its own
A thin vertical line followed by a thicker vertical line
A thick vertical line followed by a thin vertical line

items.prompt: An ordinary bar line and a final bar line both mean the music has ended.
items.explain: An ordinary bar line simply separates two bars, and the music continues. Only the final bar line (thin + thick) signals that the piece is finished.

items.prompt: You are reading a piece of music and you spot a final bar line. What should you do when you reach it?
items.explain: The final bar line is the definitive signal that the music is over. When you reach it, you stop playing.
options: Skip to the next line and keep playing
Pause briefly, then continue into the next bar
Stop playing, because the piece has ended
Repeat the previous bar

blocks.title: Check your understanding: The Final Bar Line

blocks.text: Putting It All Together at the Piano

blocks.md:
You have learned what a beat is, how beats group into bars, and what bar lines look like on the page. Now it is time to bring all of that together with your hands on the keys.

The short exercise below uses just four notes: **C, D, E, and F**. Find them on your keyboard now.

blocks.label: The four notes you will use: C, D, E, F

blocks.md: The exercise is **four bars long**. Each bar has **four beats**. That makes sixteen beats in total. You play fifteen notes: most last one beat, and the final C is held for two beats. The time signature (the two numbers at the start) is **4/4**, which simply means "four beats in every bar".

**A quick reminder of the terms on the page:**
- **Bar line:** the vertical line that separates one bar from the next.
- **Final bar line:** the thick pair of lines at the very end, telling you the music is finished.
- **Time signature (4/4):** the numbers at the start that tell you there are four beats per bar.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C clef=treble
C D E F | F E D C | C E C E | F D C2 |]
blocks.caption: Your four-bar exercise. Each quarter note (crotchet) is one beat. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" steadily in each bar. The single bar lines divide the music into four equal bars. The final bar line at the end tells you the exercise is complete.

blocks.md: Listen to the exercise all the way through before you play it yourself. Notice how it feels like it moves in steady groups of four.
Work through the steps below one at a time. There is no rush.
Place your right-hand thumb on **middle C** (C4). This is the first note of bar 1. Rest your fingers loosely over D, E, and F so each finger is already close to its note.
blocks.title: Step 1: Find your starting note

blocks.md: Before you play a single note, count "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud at a slow, steady speed. This is called counting yourself in. It sets your pulse before the music begins. Try tapping your foot or nodding your head on each count to feel the beat in your body.
blocks.title: Step 2: Count a free bar before you start

blocks.md:
Play each note exactly on the count. Say the number as your finger goes down:

- **Bar 1:** C (1) D (2) E (3) F (4)
- **Bar 2:** F (1) E (2) D (3) C (4)
- **Bar 3:** C (1) E (2) C (3) E (4)
- **Bar 4:** F (1) D (2) C (3 and 4, held for two beats)

Keep your voice and your finger moving at exactly the same moment.
blocks.title: Step 3: Play and count aloud together

blocks.md: If you find yourself rushing, slow down until every beat feels equal. A steady slow tempo is far more useful than a fast uneven one. Think of a clock ticking: every tick is the same length as the last.

Each time you finish counting "4", you cross a bar line on the page and the next bar begins on "1" again.

When you play the very last note you will see the final bar line.
blocks.title: Step 4: Spot the bar lines and final bar line as you play

blocks.md:
**Your practice task:**

1. Open the notation above so you can see the music while you play.
2. Count yourself in with a free bar of "1, 2, 3, 4".
3. Play all four bars, counting aloud on every beat.
4. After you finish, point to each bar line on the screen and count how many there are. Then point to the final bar line at the end.
5. Play the exercise two more times, aiming to keep the tempo exactly the same from the first note to the last.

Challenge: can you play it without looking at your hand? Keep your eyes on the notation instead.

**What you just did:**
You read notation, felt the pulse in groups of four, played across four bars, and identified bar lines and a final bar line in real music. That is everything this lesson is about, working together at once. Well done.

items.prompt: Look at the exercise above. How many bar lines (not counting the final bar line at the end) are there in the four-bar exercise?
items.explain: A four-bar piece has three bar lines separating the bars, plus a final bar line at the very end. The final bar line is not counted as a regular bar line.

items.prompt: In the exercise, bar 4 ends with the note C held for two beats. What does the symbol at the very end of bar 4 tell you?
items.explain: The final bar line always marks the end of a piece or section of music. It tells the player that the music is complete.
options: Repeat the exercise from the beginning
Pause and wait for the teacher
The music is finished
Play the next bar more quietly

items.prompt: When you count yourself in with a free bar before playing, you are setting a steady pulse so your first note arrives on time.
items.explain: Counting a free bar in before you play gives you time to feel the tempo in your body. Your first note then lands exactly on beat 1, already in time.

blocks.md: Every piece of sheet music you will ever read is divided into bars by bar lines. When you sit down at the piano and count "one, two, three, four" before you play, you are feeling the beat. When you tap your foot along to a song, you are tracking the beat. The moment you begin reading music or playing with another person, bars and bar lines become your map. They tell you exactly where you are in the music, where the strong beat lands, and when a section ends. Even the very first absolute beginner pieces in the pieces library use bar lines, so recognising them now means nothing will look unfamiliar when you meet real music on the page.

- **Beat**: the steady, repeating pulse that runs through a piece of music, like a ticking clock or a heartbeat.
- **Strong beat**: the beat that feels like a natural emphasis or accent, normally the first beat of each group.
- **Weak beat**: the beats that follow the strong beat within a group; they feel lighter by comparison.
- **Bar (also called a measure)**: a small group of beats enclosed between two bar lines, always containing the same number of beats throughout a piece.
- **Bar line**: a vertical line drawn across the stave (the set of five lines music is written on) to mark the end of one bar and the start of the next.
- **Final bar line**: a thin vertical line immediately followed by a thick one, marking the very end of a piece.

- A beat is the steady pulse of music. It stays even, like a clock.
- Beats have weight: the first beat of each group is strong, the rest are weak.
- Beats are grouped together into bars, each bar holding the same number of beats.
- Bar lines are the vertical lines on the stave that separate one bar from the next.
- A final bar line signals the end of a piece.
- Counting beats in groups and watching for bar lines keeps you on track at the piano.

items.prompt: What is a beat in music?
items.explain: A beat is the steady, repeating pulse that underlies music, like the ticking of a clock or a heartbeat. Loud notes, bars, and stave symbols are all separate ideas.
options: A loud note played on the piano
A steady, repeating pulse that runs through a piece of music
The space between two bar lines
A symbol written on the stave

items.prompt: In a group of four beats, beat 1 is the strongest beat.
items.explain: Beat 1 is always the strong beat that starts a new bar. The beats that follow (2, 3, 4) are weaker by comparison, which is what gives music its sense of rhythm and flow.

items.prompt: What does a bar line do?
items.explain: A bar line is a vertical line drawn across the stave that divides the music into bars, each containing the same number of beats. It is not a volume instruction, an ending marker, or a hand guide.
options: It tells you how loud to play
It marks the end of a piece of music
It separates beats into evenly sized groups called bars
It shows you which notes to play with your right hand

items.prompt: A final bar line (two vertical lines at the end of a piece) tells you that the music has done what?
items.explain: A final bar line signals the end of a piece of music. It is the musical equivalent of a full stop at the end of a sentence.

items.prompt: Every bar in a piece of music contains the same number of beats.
items.explain: Once a grouping is set (for example, three beats per bar or four beats per bar), every bar in that piece contains that same number of beats. This consistency is what lets musicians keep their place in the music.
